opus-5.5.text:
I think the first thing is to be honest about where the evidence actually stands. We've had some genuinely encouraging results. Filtering out certain categories of dual-use content, like detailed bioweapons-relevant material, before pre-training seems to produce models that are meaningfully worse at those specific tasks. They're also more robust to fine-tuning attacks than models that only had safety training applied afterward. That robustness is the key selling point. Post-training refusals are a thin veneer. If the knowledge was never learned in the first place, it's much harder to elicit.

But going from "this works in a research setting at moderate scale" to "frontier developers do this by default" requires a few things.

One is cost evidence. Labs need to know what they're giving up. Does filtering degrade general capabilities, or capabilities in adjacent beneficial domains? If you strip out a lot of virology, do you hurt the model's usefulness for legitimate biomedical research? The early results suggest the capability tax is small, but small at one scale isn't necessarily small at the frontier. So I'd want to see replications at larger scales, ideally by more than one group.

The second is tooling. Right now, building good classifiers to identify hazardous content in a multi-trillion-token corpus is bespoke work. If you want broad adoption, you want something closer to shared infrastructure: well-validated classifiers, agreed-upon taxonomies of what counts as hazardous, benchmarks for measuring whether the filtering actually took. That lowers the barrier for labs that don't have a big safety team, and it's especially important for open-weight developers. There, pre-training interventions are arguably the only safety measure that really survives release.

The third piece is incentives and norms. Some of this can come from voluntary commitments. Frontier safety frameworks could explicitly list data filtering as a mitigation for certain risk thresholds. But I think there's also a role for government or third-party evaluators to treat it as an expected practice, in the same way we expect red-teaming now. You don't necessarily need a mandate right away. Making it legible, something labs report on and evaluators check, shifts the default.

And finally, I'd be careful not to oversell it. Filtering is not a complete solution. Models can sometimes reconstruct knowledge from adjacent material, and with tool use and retrieval, a model might just look things up. So I'd position it as one layer in a defense-in-depth approach, a layer with a particularly nice property: it's hard to undo. Presenting it that way is both more accurate and, I think, more persuasive to the people who actually have to make these training decisions.

r001.rationale: The response calls for larger-scale replications but does not identify repeated experiments as financially feasible for a nonprofit.

r002.rationale: It asks for evidence about capability costs and larger-scale replication, but does not make adoption conditional on favorable experimental scaling laws.

r003.rationale: It does not propose gradually increasing the fraction of pre-training data filtered.

r004.rationale: It says filtering is especially important for open-weight developers because it survives release, but does not predict they will adopt it first.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that the research is further along than the adoption, and the gap is mostly not a technical one. We and a few other groups have now shown fairly convincingly that if you filter out, say, biosecurity or cyber-offense content from the pre-training corpus, you get a model that's much more robust to jailbreaks and fine-tuning attacks on those topics, and you pay a pretty small capability tax, often within noise on general benchmarks. So the experiments exist. The question is why isn't every frontier lab doing this by default, and how do you get there.

The first thing I'd do is get the cost story really nailed down at scale. Most of the published work, including ours, is on models that are small by frontier standards, a few billion parameters, and labs reasonably ask whether the results transfer. They worry that at trillion-token scale, a classifier-based filter either becomes expensive to run over the whole corpus, or it's too aggressive and removes a lot of adjacent benign content like chemistry textbooks or security blog posts, and you end up with a model that's worse at legitimate things. So I'd want to be running the filtering at full corpus scale, ideally in partnership with a lab, and showing the tax really is low. Running a cheap classifier over a corpus is actually a small fraction of pre-training compute, so I don't think the compute cost is the real blocker, but you have to demonstrate it rather than assert it.

The second thing is making it cheap to adopt in an engineering sense. Labs already have data pipelines with lots of filters in them, for quality, deduplication, toxicity, PII. Pre-training safety filtering should look like one more stage in that pipeline, not a research project. So I'd want open-source classifiers, documented thresholds, evaluation suites that let a lab check they haven't degraded the model, and ideally some shared datasets of what counts as hazardous content in each domain. The less a lab has to build from scratch, the more likely someone just turns it on.

Third, and this is where I think the real leverage is, you want the external pressure aligned with it. Right now a lot of safety cases for frontier models rest on post-training refusals plus some monitoring, and everyone knows refusals are fragile. If evaluators, whether that's government AI safety institutes or third-party auditors, start asking "what have you done so the dangerous knowledge isn't in the weights in the first place," then filtering becomes part of how you pass a review rather than a nice-to-have. I'd push on that in things like the frontier safety frameworks and the various codes of practice, because it's a concrete, measurable mitigation in a field where most of the mitigations are hard to measure.

And then I'd be candid about the limitations, because overselling it would hurt adoption more than help. Filtering doesn't make a model incapable of reasoning about a dangerous topic from first principles, and a determined actor with fine-tuning access and their own data can still put the knowledge back. It raises the cost, it doesn't eliminate the risk. It also really only works for narrow, well-defined hazard categories where you can write a classifier, like specific dual-use bio or weapons content. It's not going to solve something like deception or power-seeking, which aren't about any particular document being in the corpus. So I'd frame it as a defense-in-depth layer, stacked with post-training and with monitoring, rather than a replacement for them.

If I had to bet on what actually gets it adopted, it's one lab doing it publicly on a frontier model and showing no meaningful capability hit. Once that happens the argument that it's too costly goes away, and the question for everyone else becomes why they aren't doing it. That tends to be how safety practices spread in this industry, more by competitive precedent than by anyone being persuaded in the abstract.

r002.rationale: It recommends demonstrating low capability cost at scale, but does not make adoption conditional on favorable experimental scaling laws.

astra-6.text:
I’d approach it in stages. First, I’d want to establish that the filtering actually produces the behavior we care about, rather than just making a particular benchmark look better. If you remove certain information from pre-training, can the model still infer it from what remains? And how easily does that capability come back with fine-tuning?

Then there’s the question of cost. Does the filtering degrade useful capabilities? How much additional work does it introduce into the training pipeline? A convincing demonstration would show a meaningful safety benefit while keeping those costs manageable.

For wider adoption, I’d try to make it easy for a training team to run a comparison on their own data. Provide a reproducible filtering procedure and evaluations, then work up from smaller runs to larger ones. I wouldn’t expect people to change a major pre-training run on the strength of one experiment.

And I’d treat filtering as one layer of protection. The case for adopting it doesn’t have to be that it solves the whole problem. It needs to provide a measurable benefit, survive attempts to circumvent it, and fit alongside the other safeguards people are using.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d start by trying to make the empirical case stronger. If you filter out some category of pre-training data, how reliably does that reduce the corresponding capability? And what happens to the capabilities you actually want to preserve? You’d want to test that across model sizes and datasets, because a result on a small model might not survive scaling.

Then I’d work with a lab to run a pilot in a real training pipeline. That gives you a chance to understand the practical costs and to check whether the model can recover the capability during fine-tuning, or learn it from material that slipped through the filter.

If those results are promising, the next step is to make adoption straightforward: provide filtering tools, clear evaluations, and evidence about the trade-offs. I’d see this as one layer of a safety strategy. The goal is to establish where filtering provides a meaningful reduction in risk, and give labs a practical reason to use it.
